title: When Tests Disagree: Lupus Anticoagulant, LAHPS and Bleeding with a Normal Screen
summary: Learn why a lupus anticoagulant prolongs clotting tests but is linked to thrombosis, why its hypoprothrombinemia variant bleeds, and what to consider when a patient bleeds despite a normal PT, APTT, platelet count and von Willebrand factor: vessel-wall disorders and fast clot lysis.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 36 Hit 12 (lupus anticoagulant misnomer and LAHPS), Trap 1 (LA does not mean bleeding), Hit 16 (bleeding with normal platelets, PT, APTT and VWF) and Hit 17 (normal routine labs with fast clot lysis). Checked against Vandevelde & Devreese 2022, Marco-Rico 2025, Molinari 2023, Omer 2022, Sakamoto 2021, Mehic 2023, Leinøe 2024, Valke 2022, Haisma 2026, Mohammed 2021 and Pishko 2022 (full texts via Europe PMC). Hit 12 says LA is “mostly non-SLE”; the sources read say only that LA was named after SLE and is also found outside SLE, so “mostly” is not taught (register flag rv-ch36-la-non-sle-share). Trap 1 and Hit 12 say LAHPS responds to corticosteroids; Omer 2022 notes there are no guidelines, corticosteroids are the usual standard, drug- and infection-associated cases may resolve on their own, and thrombosis followed in 13% in one review (register flag rv-ch36-lahps-context). Hit 16 equates a normal screen with a vascular wall disorder; Mehic 2023 lists vessel and connective-tissue mimics but also fibrinolytic disorders and reports 50–70% bleeding disorder of unknown cause after full workup (register flag rv-ch36-normal-screen-ddx). Hit 17 relies on a short euglobulin lysis time; Valke 2022 found most presumptive fibrinolytic disorders through the ECLT ratio before and after venous compression (only 5 had a short baseline ECLT), the ECLT is not commercially available, and PAI-1 needs specific antigen assays on morning samples (Haisma 2026) (register flag rv-ch36-hyperfibrinolysis-tests). Not taught: the 2–5 h euglobulin lysis reference range, α2-antiplasmin concentration, and the “normal clots do not lyse at 24 h” statement.

objectives: Explain why a lupus anticoagulant prolongs phospholipid-dependent clotting tests yet is associated with thrombosis.
Describe the mechanism, typical patient and laboratory pattern of lupus anticoagulant–hypoprothrombinemia syndrome.
List vessel-wall and fibrinolytic causes of bleeding with a normal PT, APTT, platelet count and VWF, and the tests and first-line treatment for hyperfibrinolysis.

cues.text: Three coagulation puzzles. First, a young adult with two venous clots, and a long APTT that does not correct when mixed with normal plasma.

Second, a six-year-old with nosebleeds after a viral illness, a long PT and APTT, and a positive lupus anticoagulant. Third, an adult who bled hours after a tooth extraction, with completely normal screening tests.
In each case, do the tests match the bleeding?

scenes.title: A lupus anticoagulant clots, not bleeds
scenes.altText: Schematic: four cards on lupus anticoagulant (LA). Target card: a mixed family of autoantibodies against phospholipids and phospholipid-bound proteins such as β2-glycoprotein I and prothrombin (Marco-Rico 2025; Molinari 2023). Tube card: the antibodies compete with clotting factors for reagent phospholipid, prolonging phospholipid-dependent tests, usually the APTT; the high phospholipid content of routine PT reagents means LA rarely prolongs the routine PT. Body card: in patients LA is linked to thrombosis, not bleeding, so the name is a misnomer; it was named after systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) but is also found outside SLE (Vandevelde & Devreese 2022). Lab card: screen, mix, confirm with excess phospholipid; ISTH guidance runs dRVVT and an APTT-based test in parallel; for antiphospholipid syndrome the result must persist on repeat testing at least 12 weeks apart.

cues.text: A lupus anticoagulant is a mixed family of autoantibodies against phospholipids and the proteins that bind them, such as beta-2 glycoprotein one and prothrombin.

In the tube, the antibodies compete with clotting factors for reagent phospholipid, so phospholipid-dependent tests, usually the APTT, run long. Routine PT reagents contain so much phospholipid that the PT is rarely affected.
In the body, the same antibody is linked to thrombosis, not bleeding, so the name misleads. It was named after lupus, but it also turns up in people without lupus.

The lab screens, mixes, and confirms with extra phospholipid, usually running a dilute Russell viper venom time and an APTT side by side. For antiphospholipid syndrome, a positive result must persist at least twelve weeks later.

props.title: In the body
lines: Named for lupus, not limited to it

scenes.title: The bleeding exception
scenes.altText: Schematic mechanism chain for lupus anticoagulant–hypoprothrombinemia syndrome (LAHPS): high-affinity, non-neutralizing anti-prothrombin antibody binds prothrombin in the circulation → immune complex is cleared by the monocyte–macrophage system → low prothrombin (factor II) activity → bleeding, which can be severe (Marco-Rico 2025; Sakamoto 2021). Who card: found mainly in children with LA, sometimes after viral infection; usually associated with autoimmune disease, especially SLE (Sakamoto 2021; Omer 2022). Lab card: PT and APTT prolonged, LA positive, low factor II; in the Omer 2022 case neither the PT nor the APTT corrected on 1:1 mixing. Treatment card: no guidelines; corticosteroids are the usual standard (in a 77-patient review, 60% received them, most often prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day); drug- and infection-associated cases may resolve on their own; thrombosis was reported in 13% after the bleeding presentation in another review (Omer 2022).

cues.text: Now the exception. In lupus anticoagulant hypoprothrombinemia syndrome, a non-neutralizing antibody binds prothrombin in the blood. The immune complex is cleared, so prothrombin, factor two, falls, and the patient bleeds.
It is found mainly in children with a lupus anticoagulant, sometimes after a viral infection, and is often linked to autoimmune disease, especially lupus.
The PT and APTT are both long, factor two is low, and the lupus anticoagulant is positive. In one reported case, mixing corrected neither test.

There are no formal guidelines; corticosteroids are the usual treatment, and infection-linked cases may settle on their own. That is the hook’s second case. Some patients later develop thrombosis, so follow-up matters.

props.label: Corticosteroids usual · infection cases may self-resolve

scenes.title: Normal screen, real bleeding
scenes.altText: Three cards. Screen card: PT, APTT, platelet count and von Willebrand factor (VWF) tests can all be normal in a true bleeding tendency; after a full specialist workup, 50–70% of patients with mild-to-moderate bleeding still have a bleeding disorder of unknown cause (Mehic 2023). Vessel card: conditions that mimic a bleeding disorder include scurvy (perifollicular haemorrhage, gum disease, poor wound healing), Ehlers–Danlos and other connective-tissue disorders (fragile vessel wall from abnormal collagen), vasculitis such as Henoch–Schönlein purpura, and hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Mehic 2023; Leinøe 2024). Lysis card: PAI-1 inhibits tPA and urokinase; α2-antiplasmin binds plasmin directly; deficiency of either speeds clot breakdown, giving mucosal and delayed bleeding after trauma, surgery or tooth extraction with normal routine coagulation tests (Valke 2022; Haisma 2026; Mohammed 2021 case). These disorders are rare (Mehic 2023). Tests: euglobulin clot lysis time, ideally as a ratio before and after venous compression, plus PAI-1 antigen and activity on morning samples and α2-antiplasmin; these assays are specialised and not standardised. Treatment: tranexamic acid, a lysine analogue that blocks fibrin binding sites, was the first-line treatment for all presumptive fibrinolytic disorders in Valke 2022. Hook answers: (1) lupus anticoagulant, thrombotic; (2) LAHPS, bleeds from low prothrombin; (3) normal screen: look at the vessel wall and fibrinolysis.

cues.text: Now the reverse problem: real bleeding with a normal PT, APTT, platelet count and von Willebrand factor. Among patients referred with mild to moderate bleeding, half or more have no cause found even after a full workup.

Check the vessel wall and connective tissue: scurvy, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, vasculitis such as Henoch-Schönlein purpura, and hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia are causes of bleeding outside the clotting system that should be ruled out.

Then check clot breakdown. PAI-1 blocks plasminogen activators and alpha-2 antiplasmin blocks plasmin. If either is missing, the clot breaks down too early, causing delayed bleeding. These disorders are rare, specialised lysis tests are needed, and tranexamic acid is the usual first treatment.
Back to the hook. Case one: a lupus anticoagulant, with clots. Case two: hypoprothrombinemia syndrome, which bleeds. Case three: a normal screen, so check the vessel wall and fibrinolysis.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A lupus anticoagulant means the patient will bleed” (✓ it is linked to thrombosis; the bleeding exception is LAHPS with low prothrombin); “Normal PT, APTT, platelets and VWF rule out a bleeding disorder” (✓ vessel-wall, connective-tissue and fibrinolytic disorders, and many unexplained cases, have normal screens); “Fast clot lysis shows up on the routine PT and APTT” (✓ routine tests are typically normal; specialised lysis tests and PAI-1 or α2-antiplasmin levels are needed).

cues.text: Trap one: a lupus anticoagulant means the patient will bleed. No: it is linked to thrombosis. The bleeding exception is the hypoprothrombinemia syndrome.
Trap two: normal screening tests rule out a bleeding disorder. No: vessel-wall and fibrinolytic disorders, and many unexplained cases, have normal screens.
Trap three: fast clot breakdown shows up on the PT and APTT. No: those are typically normal; specialised lysis tests are needed.

props.title: ✗ “A lupus anticoagulant means bleeding.”
lines: ✓ Thrombosis; LAHPS (low FII) is the exception

props.title: ✗ “Fast lysis shows on PT and APTT.”
lines: ✓ Routine tests typically normal; use lysis tests

scenes.title: Long tube, clotted body
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Lupus anticoagulant: long in the tube, clots in the body — unless it carries prothrombin away, then it bleeds. Normal tube, bleeding body: look at the wall and the wrecking crew (fibrinolysis).” Tokens: long tube = clots · low II = bleeds · normal tube = wall or lysis. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: lupus anticoagulant is long in the tube but clots in the body, unless it carries prothrombin away, and then it bleeds. A normal tube with a bleeding patient means check the wall and the wrecking crew, fibrinolysis.

Where it breaks: a lupus anticoagulant does not always prolong the APTT, because reagents differ; the bleeding syndrome can later clot; and many normal-screen bleeders have platelet function problems or no cause found.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Lupus anticoagulant: long APTT · thrombosis · LAHPS (low FII) bleeds”, “Normal screen + bleeding → vessel wall or fibrinolysis · tranexamic acid”.

cues.text: A lupus anticoagulant lengthens clotting times in the tube but is linked to thrombosis in the body unless an anti-prothrombin antibody clears prothrombin, and a patient who bleeds despite normal screening tests still needs a look at the vessel wall and at fibrinolysis, where tranexamic acid is the usual first treatment.

props.label: Lupus anticoagulant: long APTT · thrombosis · LAHPS (low FII) bleeds
Normal screen + bleeding → vessel wall or fibrinolysis · tranexamic acid

explanation.what: Plain language: sometimes the clotting tests and the patient disagree. A lupus anticoagulant makes tube tests slow but makes real clots more likely; one rare form removes prothrombin and causes bleeding. And some people bleed even though every routine test is normal, because the problem is in the vessel wall or in clots breaking down too fast. Scientific terms: antiphospholipid antibodies, β2-glycoprotein I, prothrombin (factor II), dilute Russell viper venom time (dRVVT), lupus anticoagulant–hypoprothrombinemia syndrome (LAHPS), bleeding disorder of unknown cause (BDUC), plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1), α2-antiplasmin, euglobulin clot lysis time (ECLT), tranexamic acid.
explanation.why: LA antibodies bind phospholipid-bound proteins and compete with clotting factors for reagent phospholipid, slowing phospholipid-dependent tests, while in vivo they are linked to thrombosis. In LAHPS a non-neutralizing anti-prothrombin antibody forms immune complexes that are cleared, so factor II falls and bleeding follows. With a normal screen, bleeding can come from fragile vessels or connective tissue (scurvy, Ehlers–Danlos, vasculitis, telangiectasia) or from loss of fibrinolysis inhibitors: PAI-1 normally blocks tPA and urokinase, and α2-antiplasmin blocks plasmin.
explanation.measure: LA: screen, mix, confirm with excess phospholipid; dRVVT plus an APTT-based test; persistence at least 12 weeks apart for APS; routine PT rarely prolonged. LAHPS: prolonged PT and APTT, low factor II, LA positive (in the Omer 2022 case neither corrected on mixing). Hyperfibrinolysis: routine PT, APTT, platelet count and VWF normal; ECLT (ideally as a ratio before and after venous compression), PAI-1 antigen and activity on morning samples, α2-antiplasmin activity; assays are specialised and not standardised.
explanation.differs: LA in APS (linked to thrombosis) vs LAHPS (bleeding, low factor II); vessel-wall bleeding (purpura, connective-tissue signs) vs fibrinolytic bleeding (clot forms then dissolves, delayed bleeding after surgery or extraction); true normal-screen disorders vs bleeding disorder of unknown cause.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: a long APTT with thrombosis (LA, not a bleeding risk), a child with LA, bleeding and low factor II (LAHPS; corticosteroids are the usual, not guideline-based, treatment), mucocutaneous bleeding with normal screens (think vessel wall), and delayed bleeding with normal screens and fast lysis (rare hyperfibrinolysis, tranexamic acid).

mnemonic.text: Lupus anticoagulant: long in the tube, clots in the body — unless it carries prothrombin away, then it bleeds. Normal tube, bleeding body: check the wall and the wrecking crew (fibrinolysis).
mnemonic.explanation: Links the test result to the clinical direction and names the two places to look when routine tests are normal.

takeaway: A lupus anticoagulant lengthens clotting times in the tube but is linked to thrombosis in the body unless an anti-prothrombin antibody clears prothrombin, and a patient who bleeds despite normal screening tests still needs a look at the vessel wall and at fibrinolysis, where tranexamic acid is the usual first treatment.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old has had two unprovoked venous thromboses. The APTT is prolonged, does not correct on 1:1 mixing, and shortens when excess phospholipid is added. What best explains these findings?

options.text: Lupus anticoagulant, which is associated with thrombosis
options.rationale: Correct. The antibodies slow phospholipid-dependent tests in vitro, and excess phospholipid overcomes them, but in patients they are linked to thrombosis.

options.text: Factor VIII deficiency with a bleeding risk
options.rationale: Incorrect. A factor deficiency is expected to correct when mixed 1:1 with normal plasma, and here mixing did not correct; factor VIII deficiency also does not explain thrombosis.

options.text: Acquired factor VIII inhibitor causing thrombosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. A factor VIII inhibitor (acquired haemophilia A) can also give a long APTT that does not correct on mixing, and some even mimic LA in confirm tests, but it causes bleeding, not thrombosis.

options.text: Factor XII deficiency causing the clots
options.rationale: Incorrect. Factor XII deficiency is a factor deficiency, so the APTT would be expected to correct on 1:1 mixing, which did not happen here.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old has nosebleeds after a viral illness. PT and APTT are prolonged and do not correct on mixing, the lupus anticoagulant is positive, and factor II activity is low. What mechanism best explains the bleeding?

options.text: A non-neutralizing anti-prothrombin antibody forms immune complexes that are cleared, lowering prothrombin
options.rationale: Correct. This is lupus anticoagulant–hypoprothrombinemia syndrome; clearance of antibody–prothrombin complexes lowers factor II and causes bleeding.

options.text: The lupus anticoagulant neutralizes reagent phospholipid in the body
options.rationale: Incorrect. Competition for phospholipid explains the prolonged tube tests, not bleeding; the usual lupus anticoagulant is linked to thrombosis.

options.text: Vitamin K deficiency after the infection
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lack of vitamin K lowers several vitamin K–dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X), not factor II alone, and a factor deficiency is expected to correct on mixing; it does not explain a positive lupus anticoagulant.
Incorrect. Haemophilia A is a factor VIII deficiency: it would be expected to correct on mixing and does not explain low factor II or a positive lupus anticoagulant.

questions.stem: A patient bleeds again several hours after a tooth extraction. PT, APTT, platelet count and von Willebrand factor tests are normal. The euglobulin clot lysis time ratio is increased and PAI-1 antigen and activity are both low. Which treatment fits best as first line?

options.rationale: Correct. It is a lysine analogue that blocks fibrin binding sites and inhibits fibrinolysis; it was the first-line treatment for presumptive fibrinolytic disorders in the cohort read.
Incorrect. The PT is normal, so nothing points to a vitamin K–dependent factor deficiency; the problem is early clot breakdown.
Incorrect. The platelet count is normal and the defect is premature clot breakdown, not platelet number.
Incorrect. Heparin is an anticoagulant; it does nothing to stop early clot breakdown and is not a treatment for bleeding.

claims.text: LA is a heterogeneous group of antibodies against phospholipids and phospholipid-bound proteins (β2-glycoprotein I, prothrombin) that prolong phospholipid-dependent tests, usually the APTT, and rarely the routine PT.
LA is associated with thrombosis rather than bleeding (a misnomer) and was named after SLE but is also found outside SLE.
Screen, mix and confirm with excess phospholipid; dRVVT and an APTT-based test in parallel; persistence at least 12 weeks apart for APS laboratory criteria.

A factor deficiency is expected to correct on 1:1 mixing with normal plasma, an inhibitor is not; factor VIII inhibitors (acquired haemophilia A) give a non-correcting APTT, can mimic LA, and cause bleeding; vitamin K antagonists lower factors II, VII, IX and X.

LAHPS: non-neutralizing anti-prothrombin antibody, immune-complex clearance, low factor II and bleeding; mainly children, sometimes after viral infection, often with autoimmune disease or SLE; prolonged PT and APTT with LA positive (neither corrected on mixing in the Omer 2022 case).
No guidelines; corticosteroids are the usual standard; drug- and infection-associated cases may resolve spontaneously; thrombosis can follow the bleeding presentation.

Bleeding with normal routine tests: vessel and connective-tissue mimics (scurvy, Ehlers–Danlos, vasculitis such as Henoch–Schönlein purpura, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia); 50–70% remain unexplained after a workup that also excludes platelet function defects.

PAI-1 inhibits tPA and urokinase; α2-antiplasmin inhibits plasmin; deficiencies are rare and give mucosal and delayed bleeding with normal routine coagulation tests and need specialised assays (ECLT, ideally as a ratio after venous compression; PAI-1 antigen on morning samples; α2-antiplasmin).
Tranexamic acid, a lysine analogue blocking fibrin binding sites, is the usual first treatment for presumptive fibrinolytic disorders.
LA patients are “mostly non-SLE”; euglobulin lysis time reference 2–5 h; α2-antiplasmin plasma concentration; normal clots do not lyse even at 24 h.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 36 Hit 12 says lupus anticoagulant is “mostly non-SLE”. The sources read (Vandevelde & Devreese 2022; Marco-Rico 2025) say only that LA was named after SLE and is also found in other conditions; none gave the share of LA-positive patients without SLE, so the lesson teaches “not limited to SLE” (register flag rv-ch36-la-non-sle-share).

Ch. 36 Hit 12 and Trap 1 present LAHPS as a childhood bleeding syndrome that responds to corticosteroids. Omer 2022 adds that there are no treatment guidelines (corticosteroids are the usual standard), drug- and infection-associated cases can resolve spontaneously, LAHPS is usually associated with autoimmune disease such as SLE, and thrombosis followed the bleeding presentation in 13% in one review (register flag rv-ch36-lahps-context).

Ch. 36 Hit 16 equates bleeding with normal platelets, PT, APTT and VWF with a vascular wall disorder. Mehic 2023 lists vessel and connective-tissue mimics but also hyperfibrinolytic and other rare disorders not detected by routine tests, and reports that 50–70% of patients with mild-to-moderate bleeding remain a bleeding disorder of unknown cause after full workup (register flag rv-ch36-normal-screen-ddx).

Ch. 36 Hit 17 diagnoses hyperfibrinolysis from a short euglobulin lysis time. Valke 2022 found most presumptive fibrinolytic disorders by the ECLT ratio before and after venous compression (only 5 of 63 had a short baseline ECLT), notes the ECLT is not commercially available and fibrinolytic assays are not standardised; Haisma 2026 requires PAI-1 antigen on morning samples because activity assays cannot reliably detect low values (register flag rv-ch36-hyperfibrinolysis-tests).
